observed.title: 63. 电视

paragraphs.text:
电视技术把图像信息从一个地方传送到另一个地方。
本课介绍的是早期模拟电视中的无线电传输、摄像管和显像管原理，而不是所有现代电视系统的统一结构。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
在本课介绍的模拟电视系统中，发射端先把图像转变成随时间连续变化的电信号，再用这个信号调制高频振荡。
调制后的电磁波把图像信息带到远处，接收机检波取得图像信号，再把它还原成可见图像。
运动图像由连续传送的画面形成：每秒传送几十幅只有较小变化的画面，观看时便能呈现运动；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 这个描述不规定所有系统都采用同一种画面速率。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
教材介绍的**光电摄像管**把图像转变成一系列电信号（图 125）。
光学系统把物体的像投影到由许多感光小单元组成的镶嵌屏上，各单元的电荷状态与受到的光照有关。
电子枪发出的电子束依次扫描一行中的各单元，再扫描下一行。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
电子束到达一个单元时，单元的电荷发生变化，产生流经电阻 $R$ 的脉冲电流。
在教材所用的近似模型中，电荷变化决定电流的大小，电阻 $R$ 上的电压变化与逐行扫描位置的照度变化成正比。
这样，图像中不同位置的明暗变化就转变成按扫描顺序排列的电信号。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
接收机检波后取得**图像信号**。
在教材介绍的**电子显像管**中，控制电极改变电子束中的电子数量，从而改变屏幕发光的明暗。
水平和竖直偏转线圈使电子束逐行扫过屏幕，对应发射端电子束扫过摄像管的镶嵌屏。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
同步信号使发射端和接收端的扫描时间与位置相互配合，才能把明暗信号放回图像中相应的位置。
这里的摄像管与显像管是早期电视设备的例子，不表示现代摄像机和屏幕都使用电子束扫描。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
教材讨论的是利用超短波、其中包括米波波段的地面电视广播，不是说电视信号只能通过这一波段传送。
这种传播通常以直线可见范围为主要条件，因此可以提高天线或设置中继发射台，扩大接收区域。
教材以莫斯科阿斯坦丁电视塔的 540 米高度和半径 120 千米的接收范围说明高塔的作用；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
这是一项历史实例，而不是任何天气和地点下的保证。
教材记述的当时电视网已有一千多个广播站和几千万台电视接收机，这些数量不是今天的统计数据。
利用转播卫星也能扩大电视广播的接收区域；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 地面广播与卫星转播的传播路径并不相同。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

调制后的电磁波把图像信息带到远处，接收机检波取得图像信号，再把它还原成可见图像。
运动图像由连续传送的画面形成：每秒传送几十幅只有较小变化的画面，观看时便能呈现运动；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text: 这个描述不规定所有系统都采用同一种画面速率。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text:
教材介绍的**光电摄像管**把图像转变成一系列电信号（图 125）。
光学系统把物体的像投影到由许多感光小单元组成的镶嵌屏上，各单元的电荷状态与受到的光照有关。
电子枪发出的电子束依次扫描一行中的各单元，再扫描下一行。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text:
电子束到达一个单元时，单元的电荷发生变化，产生流经电阻 $R$ 的脉冲电流。
在教材所用的近似模型中，电荷变化决定电流的大小，电阻 $R$ 上的电压变化与逐行扫描位置的照度变化成正比。
这样，图像中不同位置的明暗变化就转变成按扫描顺序排列的电信号。

blocks.text:
接收机检波后取得**图像信号**。
在教材介绍的**电子显像管**中，控制电极改变电子束中的电子数量，从而改变屏幕发光的明暗。
水平和竖直偏转线圈使电子束逐行扫过屏幕，对应发射端电子束扫过摄像管的镶嵌屏。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text:
同步信号使发射端和接收端的扫描时间与位置相互配合，才能把明暗信号放回图像中相应的位置。
这里的摄像管与显像管是早期电视设备的例子，不表示现代摄像机和屏幕都使用电子束扫描。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text:
教材讨论的是利用超短波、其中包括米波波段的地面电视广播，不是说电视信号只能通过这一波段传送。
这种传播通常以直线可见范围为主要条件，因此可以提高天线或设置中继发射台，扩大接收区域。
教材以莫斯科阿斯坦丁电视塔的 540 米高度和半径 120 千米的接收范围说明高塔的作用；

利用转播卫星也能扩大电视广播的接收区域；

observed.title: 63. Television

paragraphs.text: Television technology sends image information from one place to another.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: This lesson describes radio transmission, camera tubes, and picture tubes in early analog television, not a single design shared by all modern television systems.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: In the analog television system described here, the transmitter first turns an image into an electrical signal that varies continuously with time and uses it to modulate a high-frequency oscillation.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: The modulated electromagnetic wave carries the image information to a distant receiver, which detects the image signal and converts it back into a visible image.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Moving images are formed from successive pictures: dozens of slightly different pictures are transmitted each second to present motion;

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: this description does not require every system to use the same picture rate.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: The textbook's **photoelectric camera tube** converts an image into a sequence of electrical signals (Figure 125).

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: An optical system projects the object's image onto a mosaic screen made of many light-sensitive elements, whose charge states depend on the light they receive.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: The electron gun sends a beam across the elements of one row and then the next.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: When the beam reaches an element, its charge changes and produces a pulse of current through resistor $R$.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: In the textbook's approximate model, the charge change determines the current, and the voltage changes across resistor $R$ are proportional to the illumination changes along each scanned row.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Brightness differences at different image positions thus become electrical signals arranged in scanning order.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: The receiver obtains the **image signal** after detection.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: In the textbook's **electron-beam picture tube**, a control electrode changes the number of electrons in the beam and therefore the screen's brightness.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Horizontal and vertical deflection coils sweep the beam across the screen, corresponding to the transmitter's scan of the camera tube's mosaic screen.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Synchronization signals coordinate the timing and positions of the transmitting and receiving scans so that each brightness signal is placed at the correct image position.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
These camera and picture tubes are examples of early television equipment;
modern cameras and screens do not all use electron-beam scanning.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
The textbook discusses terrestrial television broadcasting using ultrashort radio waves, including the meter-wave band;
television signals are not restricted to this band.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Such propagation generally depends mainly on line of sight, so higher antennas and relay transmitters can extend the receiving area.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: The textbook uses Moscow's Ostankino television tower, with a height of 540 meters and a receiving radius of 120 kilometers, as a historical example of the role of a tall tower, not a guarantee for every weather condition or location.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
Its account of the television network at that time mentions over a thousand broadcasting stations and tens of millions of television receivers;
these are not present-day statistics.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Relay satellites can also extend television broadcasting coverage, and satellite relays use a different propagation path from terrestrial broadcasts.

texts: Television technology sends image information from one place to another.
This lesson describes radio transmission, camera tubes, and picture tubes in early analog television, not a single design shared by all modern television systems.
In the analog television system described here, the transmitter first turns an image into an electrical signal that varies continuously with time and uses it to modulate a high-frequency oscillation.
The modulated electromagnetic wave carries the image information to a distant receiver, which detects the image signal and converts it back into a visible image.
Moving images are formed from successive pictures: dozens of slightly different pictures are transmitted each second to present motion;
this description does not require every system to use the same picture rate.
The textbook's **photoelectric camera tube** converts an image into a sequence of electrical signals (Figure 125).
An optical system projects the object's image onto a mosaic screen made of many light-sensitive elements, whose charge states depend on the light they receive.
The electron gun sends a beam across the elements of one row and then the next.
When the beam reaches an element, its charge changes and produces a pulse of current through resistor $R$.
In the textbook's approximate model, the charge change determines the current, and the voltage changes across resistor $R$ are proportional to the illumination changes along each scanned row.
Brightness differences at different image positions thus become electrical signals arranged in scanning order.
Figure 125
The receiver obtains the **image signal** after detection.
In the textbook's **electron-beam picture tube**, a control electrode changes the number of electrons in the beam and therefore the screen's brightness.
Horizontal and vertical deflection coils sweep the beam across the screen, corresponding to the transmitter's scan of the camera tube's mosaic screen.
Synchronization signals coordinate the timing and positions of the transmitting and receiving scans so that each brightness signal is placed at the correct image position.

These camera and picture tubes are examples of early television equipment;
modern cameras and screens do not all use electron-beam scanning.

The textbook discusses terrestrial television broadcasting using ultrashort radio waves, including the meter-wave band;
television signals are not restricted to this band.
Such propagation generally depends mainly on line of sight, so higher antennas and relay transmitters can extend the receiving area.

The textbook uses Moscow's Ostankino television tower, with a height of 540 meters and a receiving radius of 120 kilometers, as a historical example of the role of a tall tower, not a guarantee for every weather condition or location.

Its account of the television network at that time mentions over a thousand broadcasting stations and tens of millions of television receivers;
these are not present-day statistics.
Relay satellites can also extend television broadcasting coverage, and satellite relays use a different propagation path from terrestrial broadcasts.

texts: Television technology sends image information from one place to another.
This lesson describes radio transmission, camera tubes, and picture tubes in early analog television, not a single design shared by all modern television systems.
In the analog television system described here, the transmitter first turns an image into an electrical signal that varies continuously with time and uses it to modulate a high-frequency oscillation.
The modulated electromagnetic wave carries the image information to a distant receiver, which detects the image signal and converts it back into a visible image.
Moving images are formed from successive pictures: dozens of slightly different pictures are transmitted each second to present motion;
this description does not require every system to use the same picture rate.
The textbook's **photoelectric camera tube** converts an image into a sequence of electrical signals (Figure 125).
An optical system projects the object's image onto a mosaic screen made of many light-sensitive elements, whose charge states depend on the light they receive.
The electron gun sends a beam across the elements of one row and then the next.
When the beam reaches an element, its charge changes and produces a pulse of current through resistor $R$.
In the textbook's approximate model, the charge change determines the current, and the voltage changes across resistor $R$ are proportional to the illumination changes along each scanned row.
Brightness differences at different image positions thus become electrical signals arranged in scanning order.
Figure 125
The receiver obtains the **image signal** after detection.
In the textbook's **electron-beam picture tube**, a control electrode changes the number of electrons in the beam and therefore the screen's brightness.
Horizontal and vertical deflection coils sweep the beam across the screen, corresponding to the transmitter's scan of the camera tube's mosaic screen.
Synchronization signals coordinate the timing and positions of the transmitting and receiving scans so that each brightness signal is placed at the correct image position.

These camera and picture tubes are examples of early television equipment;
modern cameras and screens do not all use electron-beam scanning.

The textbook discusses terrestrial television broadcasting using ultrashort radio waves, including the meter-wave band;
television signals are not restricted to this band.
Such propagation generally depends mainly on line of sight, so higher antennas and relay transmitters can extend the receiving area.

The textbook uses Moscow's Ostankino television tower, with a height of 540 meters and a receiving radius of 120 kilometers, as a historical example of the role of a tall tower, not a guarantee for every weather condition or location.

Its account of the television network at that time mentions over a thousand broadcasting stations and tens of millions of television receivers;
these are not present-day statistics.
Relay satellites can also extend television broadcasting coverage, and satellite relays use a different propagation path from terrestrial broadcasts.
